The vulnerability identified as CVE-2026-23871, affected WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business applications on Android devices and could have exposed users’ Internet Protocol (IP) information through specially crafted advertising reply messages containing media hosted on external websites.
WhatsApp disclosed that its security team discovered the flaw while disrupting a scam campaign, suggesting that cybercriminals may be exploiting legitimate business communication features to strengthen the credibility of fraudulent interactions.
According to a report by SecurityWeek published on November 20, 2026, the vulnerability was linked to incomplete validation of external advertising reply URLs associated with the platform’s Click to WhatsApp feature.
A WhatsApp spokesperson told the publication: “Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.”
Although the company classified the vulnerability as low impact, its discovery raises concerns about the potential consequences of security weaknesses on platforms increasingly used by businesses to communicate with customers, promote products and facilitate commercial activities.
Click to WhatsApp advertisements enable businesses to direct prospective customers from online advertisements into private conversations with their sales representatives. However, the flaw demonstrated how malicious actors could exploit weaknesses in the process to expose users’ IP information when specially crafted messages were displayed.
For Nigeria, where small businesses, online retailers, financial technology companies and service providers increasingly rely on WhatsApp to reach customers, the incident highlights the importance of treating messaging platforms as part of the country’s wider digital security infrastructure.
A fraudulent message that appears to originate from a familiar business or customer-service channel can potentially undermine trust, expose customers to phishing attempts and create opportunities for financial fraud.
The implications are particularly relevant to Nigeria’s expanding digital payments ecosystem, where customers frequently communicate with merchants, agents and service providers through messaging applications before completing transfers or other financial transactions.
While WhatsApp has not established that the vulnerability resulted in financial losses or disclosed the number of affected users, the incident reinforces the need for businesses to strengthen customer verification procedures rather than relying solely on the apparent authenticity of messages.
Furthermore, the company disclosed two additional medium-impact vulnerabilities affecting its applications, although it said it had found no evidence that either had been exploited.
One of the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-102769, involved an SQL injection weakness in WhatsApp for Android. A recipient who tapped a specially crafted order-details message sent through an unofficial client could have experienced deletion of locally stored WhatsApp files.
The other CVE-2026-44908, affected the remote-attestation verification mechanism used by WhatsApp applications to establish trust in Meta AI’s confidential computing infrastructure.
WhatsApp said it had found no evidence that either vulnerability had been exploited.
The latest disclosures underscore the need for businesses to prioritise software updates, secure customer communication channels and staff awareness as digital platforms become increasingly important to commercial activities.
Meanwhile, for Nigerian businesses using WhatsApp Business, maintaining updated applications, enabling available account security protections, verifying payment instructions through independent channels and educating employees about suspicious messages remain important safeguards against digital fraud.
Additionally, WhatsApp has urged users to keep their applications updated through official app stores and install available security updates.
